final_text: Instagram's first background-task system was Gearman. As task volume grew to thousands per second, Instagram replaced it with Celery workers and a RabbitMQ broker, as described in a PyCon 2013 talk.
note: Opened High Scalability (Instagram, Dec 2011): '200 Python workers consume tasks off the Gearman task queue'. Opened PyCon 2013 'Messaging at Scale at Instagram' (Rick Branson): 'The very first incarnation of messaging was based on Gearman', growth 'from a few jobs per minute to thousands of tasks every second', Celery + RabbitMQ.

final_text: In 2010 Facebook served over 400 billion PHP page views a month. Rather than leave PHP, it built HipHop, which turns PHP into optimised C++, cutting web-server CPU use by about half.
note: Opened engineering.fb.com (2 Feb 2010): 'over 400 billion PHP-based page views every month'; 'reduced the CPU usage on our Web servers on average by about fifty percent'. Added the ~50% figure from the page.

final_text: S3 accepts a single PUT of up to 5 GB. Multipart upload sends parts independently, in any order and in parallel, and is meant for larger objects (5 MB to 50 TB).
note: Opened S3 'Uploading objects': 'With a single PUT operation, you can upload a single object up to 5 GB'; parts 'can be uploaded independently, in any order, and in parallel'; 'objects from 5 MB to 50 TB'.

final_text: AWS does not charge for inbound data from the internet. S3 does not charge for transfer to AWS services in the same Region or to CloudFront. Data out to the internet, cross-AZ and cross-Region traffic is billed.
note: Opened AWS architecture blog: 'There is no charge for inbound data transfer across all services in all Regions'; cross-AZ and cross-Region 'typically' incur charges. S3 pricing exceptions: 'Data transferred in from the internet', 'to any AWS service(s) within the same AWS Region', 'out to Amazon CloudFront'.

final_text: A NAT gateway adds a per-GB data processing charge for traffic passing through it. A VPC gateway endpoint lets instances reach S3 in the same Region without data transfer charges.
note: Same AWS blog: NAT gateway 'data processing charge (per gigabyte (GB))'; 'VPC gateway endpoints allow communication to Amazon S3 and Amazon DynamoDB without incurring data transfer charges'.

final_text: A presigned POST policy can carry conditions such as content-length-range, Content-Type and acl. This lets the backend cap the upload size and restrict the file type even though it never sees the bytes.
note: Opened boto3 generate_presigned_post: 'Conditions that are included may pertain to acl, content-length-range, Cache-Control, Content-Type, ...'.

final_text: AWS calls presigned URLs bearer tokens: anyone who has one can use it, repeatedly, until it expires. A bucket policy can reject signatures older than a limit (the s3:signatureAge condition).
note: Opened S3 presigned URL page: 'presigned URLs are bearer tokens that grant access to those who possess them'; 'You can use the presigned URL multiple times, up to the expiration date and time'; s3:signatureAge bucket-policy example.

final_text: A presigned URL can't outlive the credentials that signed it. SDK-signed URLs can last up to 7 days with an IAM user's keys, but URLs signed with temporary role credentials expire when the role session ends (EC2 instance role credentials last about 6 hours).
note: Same page: IAM user 'Valid up to 7 days'; temporary credentials 'Can't be valid for longer than the credentials themselves'; EC2 role credentials 'typically 6 hours'.

final_text: New S3 buckets have ACLs disabled by default ('Bucket owner enforced'). Uploads that specify ACLs other than bucket-owner-full-control fail with 400 AccessControlListNotSupported. AWS recommends controlling access with bucket policies instead.
note: Opened S3 Object Ownership: 'For newly created buckets, ACLs are disabled by default'; PUTs with other ACLs 'fail and return a 400 error with the error code AccessControlListNotSupported'; recommends bucket policies.

final_text: With CloudFront origin access control, the bucket stays private. A bucket policy allows only the cloudfront.amazonaws.com service principal, for one specific distribution, to read objects.
note: Opened CloudFront 'Restrict access to an Amazon S3 origin': bucket policy allows 'the CloudFront service principal (cloudfront.amazonaws.com)' with a Condition limiting it to 'the CloudFront distribution that contains the S3 origin'.

final_text: GCS signed URLs can be valid for at most 7 days, and anyone in possession of one can use it. Azure SAS tokens are generated client-side and are not tracked by Azure Storage; Microsoft recommends user delegation SAS, signed with Entra ID credentials.
note: Opened GCS signed URLs: 'The longest expiration value is 604800 seconds (7 days)'; 'Anyone in possession of the signed URL can use it while it's active'. Azure SAS overview (updated Feb 2026): 'The SAS token is not tracked by Azure Storage in any way'; 'Microsoft recommends using a user delegation SAS', secured with Microsoft Entra credentials.

final_text: S3 Event Notifications can publish 'new object created' events to Lambda, SQS, SNS or EventBridge. Delivery is at-least-once and usually takes seconds, which is a natural trigger for asynchronous moderation of direct uploads.
note: Opened S3 Event Notifications: destinations SNS, SQS, Lambda, EventBridge; 'designed to be delivered at least once. Typically, event notifications are delivered in seconds but can sometimes take a minute or longer'.

final_text: S3 Lifecycle expiration actions delete objects on your behalf after a set age. Rules apply to a group of objects (for example a prefix used for not-yet-published uploads), so orphan cleanup needs no custom job.
note: Opened S3 Lifecycle: 'Amazon S3 deletes expired objects on your behalf'; a configuration is 'a set of rules that define actions that Amazon S3 applies to a group of objects'. The prefix example is an application of that.

final_text: By default, new S3 buckets, access points and objects don't allow public access. Block Public Access settings override bucket policies and ACLs that would make data public.
note: Opened S3 Block Public Access: 'By default, new buckets, access points, and objects don't allow public access'; 'S3 Block Public Access settings override these policies and permissions'.

final_text: GitHub limits image attachments to 10 MB. Since May 2023, new attachments in private repositories can be viewed only after logging in; GitHub's docs now say that for private and internal repositories only people with access to the repository can view uploaded files. Before the change, anyone with the direct URL could view them.
note: Opened GitHub docs: '10MB for images and gifs'; 'In the case of private and internal repositories, only people with access to the repository can view the uploaded files.' Opened changelog 2023-05-09: future attachments in private repos 'can only be viewed after logging in'; it does not mention internal repos and is not retroactive. Reworded so each claim matches its source.

final_text: Microsoft's guidance: many services use a hybrid. Some data goes through a front-end proxy that validates business rules, other data is written directly with a SAS. Data written directly should be validated before the application uses it.
note: Opened Azure SAS overview: 'Many real-world services may use a hybrid of these two approaches. For example, some data might be processed and validated via the front-end proxy. Other data is saved and/or read directly using SAS.'; 'perform that validation after the data is written and before it is used by your application'.

final_text: The name for this mapping differs by provider: Akamai calls it a property (the configuration that controls how edge servers respond to requests), and Amazon CloudFront calls it a distribution.
note: Opened Akamai key concepts: 'A property, sometimes also referred to as a configuration, provides the main way to control how edge servers respond...'. CloudFront OAC page uses 'distribution' throughout.

final_text: To use your own hostname (like edge.arpitbhayani.me), you add a DNS CNAME pointing to the CDN's edge hostname. Once the CNAME is in place, Akamai's DNS servers return the IP address of the best Akamai servers for that user.
note: Same Akamai page: 'you need a CNAME record that redirects the DNS request to the edge hostname'; 'Akamai DNS servers return the IP address of the best Akamai servers for the user's request.'

final_text: CDNs do not cache every response automatically. Cloudflare, for example, caches by file extension and does not cache HTML or JSON by default, and it skips responses marked Cache-Control private, no-store, no-cache or max-age=0, or carrying a Set-Cookie header. Cache rules or origin headers make other responses eligible.
note: Opened Cloudflare default cache behavior: 'Cloudflare only caches based on file extension and not by MIME type'; 'does not cache HTML or JSON by default'; not cached when Cache-Control is private/no-store/no-cache/max-age=0 or Set-Cookie present. Cache Rules page: adjust 'what is eligible to cache'.

final_text: How long the CDN keeps a response is set by the origin's Cache-Control max-age (or s-maxage, which CloudFront uses instead of max-age while browsers keep using max-age), bounded by the CDN's minimum and maximum TTL settings. With no cache policy and no header, CloudFront's default TTL is 24 hours.
note: Opened CloudFront Expiration: 'If you opt out of using a cache policy, the default TTL (Time to Live) is 24 hours'; table shows CloudFront uses s-maxage, browsers max-age, clamped by min/max TTL. The page does not say s-maxage applies 'only to shared caches' (that is RFC 9111 wording), so reworded to what the cited page says.

final_text: Besides waiting for the TTL or invalidating, you can give each new version of a file a new name (e.g. logo.v2.png). CloudFront recommends versioned file names for frequently updated files: they also beat browser and proxy caches and cost nothing to invalidate.
note: Opened CloudFront Invalidation: 'If you want to update your files frequently, we recommend that you primarily use file versioning'; works even behind 'a corporate caching proxy'; 'you don't have to pay for invalidating files'.

final_text: The origin does not have to be on the public internet: since November 2024, CloudFront VPC origins can deliver content from applications in a private VPC subnet.
note: Opened AWS blog dated November 20, 2024: VPC Origins 'allows users to use CloudFront to deliver content from applications hosted in a VPC private subnet'.

final_text: On AWS the native integration is origin access control (OAC): the S3 bucket stays private, its bucket policy allows the CloudFront service principal for one specific distribution, and CloudFront signs every request it sends to S3. No access keys are uploaded to the CDN.
note: Opened CloudFront OAC page: bucket policy for 'cloudfront.amazonaws.com' scoped by AWS:SourceArn to one distribution; 'it signs all requests that it sends to the S3 bucket origin' (SigV4).

final_text: S3 Standard is designed for 99.999999999% (eleven nines) durability and 99.99% availability over a year, storing objects across at least three Availability Zones.
note: Opened S3 data protection: 'Designed to provide 99.999999999% durability and 99.99% availability of objects over a given year'; 'a minimum of three Availability Zones'.

final_text: On AWS, putting CloudFront in front of S3 also changes the bill: data transfer between CloudFront and AWS origins such as S3 is waived, so you pay CloudFront's delivery price instead of S3's internet egress.
note: Opened CloudFront pricing: 'Data transfer between CloudFront and your AWS origins is automatically waived when serving traffic through CloudFront.' The waiver covers all origin fetches, not only 'cached traffic', so that phrase was removed.

final_text: As of October 2026, AWS lists two Regions in India (Mumbai and Hyderabad, three Availability Zones each), while its CDN, CloudFront, lists standard edge locations in 7 Indian cities plus embedded PoPs in 46 more.
note: Opened AWS Regions page (34 Regions): ap-south-1 Mumbai 3 AZs, ap-south-2 Hyderabad 3 AZs. Opened CloudFront features: India regular PoPs 'Bengaluru, Chennai, Hyderabad, Kolkata, Mumbai, New Delhi, Pune' (7) and 46 embedded-PoP cities. Correct as of 2026-10-13.

final_text: Per-user prefixes also help throughput: S3 supports at least 3,500 write and 5,500 read requests per second per partitioned prefix, and there is no limit on the number of prefixes in a bucket.
note: Opened S3 performance: 'at least 3,500 PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE or 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second per partitioned Amazon S3 prefix. There are no limits to the number of prefixes in a bucket.'

final_text: In CloudFront, you register public keys in a trusted key group and sign URLs with the matching private key (RSA 2048 or ECDSA 256). The CDN verifies the signature and then checks the expiry in the policy. Adding a query parameter after signing makes the URL fail with HTTP 403.
note: Opened CloudFront signed URLs: 'trusted key groups, which contain the public keys'; 'RSA 2048 and ECDSA 256'; validates signature, then the policy; 'If you add a query string to a signed URL after signing it, the URL returns an HTTP 403 status.'

final_text: The expiry is checked when each request arrives: a download that started just before expiry still completes, but a retry or a Range GET after the expiry time fails.
note: Same page: 'CloudFront checks the expiration date and time in a signed URL at the time of the HTTP request'; download started before expiry 'should complete'; 'any GET request that occurs after the expiration time passes will fail' for Range GETs.

final_text: Middle-ground options exist between 'pseudo privacy' and no CDN. CloudFront signed URLs can use a custom policy that limits access to the viewer's IP range as well as a short expiry. Signed cookies can protect many files without changing their URLs.
note: Same page: custom policy can 'specify the IP address or range of IP addresses'. Signed cookies page: for 'when you don't want to change your current URLs or when you want to provide access to multiple restricted files'.

final_text: Other CDNs offer the same idea under different names. Cloudflare's token authentication checks a URL parameter of the form verify=<issue-time>-<MAC>: it recomputes an HMAC of the path and timestamp with a shared secret and blocks the request if the MAC differs or the token is older than the allowed lifetime.
note: Opened Cloudflare token authentication: example 'verify=1484063787-...'; MAC = HMAC-SHA256 of path+timestamp with a secret; the rule blocks unless the MAC matches and 'http.request.timestamp.sec < (<TIMESTAMP_ISSUED> + 10800)'. The timestamp is the issue time, not an expiry, so reworded.

final_text: Client-chosen sizes multiply variants: Cloudflare bills each unique width produced by width=auto as a separate transformation. Cloudflare also warns not to rely on blur to hide content, because the URL can be edited to remove the blur parameter.
note: Opened Cloudflare transform-via-URL: 'each unique width counts as a separate billable transformation'; blur should not be used to obscure content as 'the URL can be modified to remove the blur parameter'. 'Many sites round widths to a few fixed sizes' is not on the page; removed.

final_text: Not every CDN has image processing built in. For Amazon CloudFront, AWS offers 'Dynamic Image Transformation for Amazon CloudFront' (formerly Serverless Image Handler), a solution you deploy in your own account: either Lambda functions using the sharp library or ECS Fargate containers, with CloudFront caching in front.
note: Opened AWS Solutions page (v8.1.2, released 10/2026): ECS Fargate architecture and Lambda architecture; 'A Lambda function ... uses sharp'; CloudFront 'provides edge caching'. sharp is named only for the Lambda variant, so reworded.

final_text: GIPHY serves its GIFs, stickers and clips through Fastly, which handles tens of billions of requests a day, with peaks of about 400,000 requests per second.
note: Opened Fastly GIPHY case study: 'tens of billions of requests daily', 'peaks reaching 400,000 requests per second'.

final_text: Netflix runs its own CDN, Open Connect. Qualifying ISPs can have Open Connect Appliances embedded in their networks at no charge, so much Netflix traffic is served from inside the viewer's ISP.
note: Opened openconnect.netflix.com: 'Open Connect Appliances can be embedded in your ISP network'; 'provided to qualifying ISP partners at no charge'; Netflix also runs OCAs in '60+ global data centers'. Reworded: not all video is served from inside the ISP.

final_text: AWS has said publicly that S3 is built on hard disk drives, millions of them, and that HDDs growing in capacity but not in speed shapes S3's design.
note: Opened All Things Distributed (Jul 2023): S3 'is built using a LOT of hard disks. Millions of them.'; 'This tension between HDDs growing in capacity but staying flat for performance is a central influence in S3's design.'

final_text: With anycast, many machines share the same IP address, and internet routing sends each user to the nearest one. So a Cloudflare user gets the same IP anywhere in the world but lands on a nearby data center.
note: Opened Cloudflare anycast primer: 'With Anycast, multiple machines can share the same IP address'; routers 'direct it to the machine on the network that is closest'.

final_text: To avoid a burst of requests to the API when the cached hashtag response expires, the origin can send Cache-Control: max-age=N, stale-while-revalidate=M. The CDN then keeps serving the stale copy for up to M seconds while it fetches a fresh one in the background.
note: Opened CloudFront Expiration: stale-while-revalidate lets CloudFront 'serve stale content from the cache while CloudFront asynchronously fetches a fresh version'; capped by the max TTL.

final_text: Kafka's broker default is log.retention.hours = 168 (7 days) with cleanup policy 'delete'. Per topic you can set retention.ms = -1 to keep data indefinitely, or use log compaction to keep the latest value per key.
note: Opened Kafka 4.1 broker configs: log.retention.hours default 168; log.retention.ms 'If set to -1, no time limit is applied'; log.cleanup.policy default delete. Re-checked Kafka 4.3 broker configs: same defaults.

final_text: In Kafka, auto.offset.reset decides where a consumer group with no committed offset starts; the default is 'latest', so a brand-new group skips existing messages unless set to 'earliest'.
note: Opened Kafka 4.1 and 4.3 consumer configs: auto.offset.reset 'What to do when there is no initial offset'; Default: latest.

final_text: Adding partitions to a Kafka topic is an online operation, but it changes the key-to-partition mapping: records with the same key may go to a different partition afterwards, and existing data is not moved.
note: Opened Kafka 4.3 basic operations: 'Kafka will not attempt to automatically redistribute existing data'; 'messages with the same key may be routed to different partitions after the expansion'.

final_text: Within a consumer group each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer, so the partition count caps how many consumers in a group can work in parallel; consumers beyond that number get no partitions.
note: Opened KafkaConsumer javadoc (4.3): 'each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in the group'; 'The number of total threads across all processes will be limited by the total number of partitions.' The page does not say 'stay idle'; reworded to follow from the stated rule.

final_text: If a counting server commits its Kafka offsets only after writing count += n to the database, a crash between the two re-processes that batch, giving at-least-once delivery and an over-count. That is exactly the recount L-0255 accepts.
note: Same javadoc: committing after processing is 'at-least-once ... as each record will likely be delivered one time but in failure cases could be duplicated'.

final_text: DynamoDB's atomic counters (UpdateItem with SET c = c + :n) are not idempotent: a retried update after a timeout can over-count. AWS suggests conditional updates where over- or under-counting can't be tolerated.
note: Opened DynamoDB 'Working with items': 'With an atomic counter, the updates are not idempotent'; retry 'would risk updating the counter twice'; 'it is safer to use a conditional update instead'.

final_text: Kafka Streams does this re-keying as a built-in step: groupBy, which picks a new key before aggregating, 'always causes data re-partitioning' by that key.
note: Opened Kafka 4.3 Streams DSL guide: 'groupBy always causes data re-partitioning'; it is shorthand for selectKey(...).groupByKey(). I could not find the 'internal repartition topic' wording for groupBy on the page (only for repartition()), so reworded.

final_text: Redis Streams, unlike Redis Pub/Sub, persist messages and support at-least-once delivery with consumer groups, so they are the Redis option when messages must survive subscriber downtime.
note: Opened Redis Pub/Sub docs: Pub/Sub is 'at-most-once'; 'Messages in streams are persisted, and support both at-most-once as well as at-least-once delivery semantics.' Consumer groups are a Streams feature (data-types page linked).

final_text: The Kafka producer already buffers unsent records in memory (buffer.memory, default 32 MiB) and retries until delivery.timeout.ms (default 120 s) before reporting failure. The 'buffer in memory' option is partly built in.
note: Opened Kafka 4.3 producer configs: buffer.memory default 33554432 (32 MiB), 'bytes of memory the producer can use to buffer records waiting to be sent'; delivery.timeout.ms default 120000, covers 'the time allowed for retriable send failures'. When the buffer is full, send() blocks for max.block.ms.

final_text: In SQS, a dead-letter queue receives messages that consumers failed to process after maxReceiveCount receives. Kafka Connect has its own DLQ setting (errors.deadletterqueue.topic.name) for records a sink connector failed to process.
note: Opened SQS DLQ: 'maxReceiveCount is the number of times a consumer can receive a message from a source queue before it is moved to a dead-letter queue'. Opened Kafka 4.3 Connect configs: DLQ 'for messages that result in an error when processed by this sink connector'. Scoped to sink connectors.

final_text: In the transactional outbox pattern, the service inserts the outgoing message into an outbox table in the same local transaction as the business update. A separate relay process then publishes it to the broker.
note: Opened microservices.io: 'first store the message in the database as part of the transaction that updates the business entities. A separate process then sends the messages to the message broker.'

final_text: Kafka tiered storage (production-ready since Kafka 3.9) moves completed log segments to remote storage such as S3 or HDFS while keeping them readable through Kafka; a RemoteStorageManager plugin must be supplied.
note: Opened Kafka 4.3 tiered storage: remote tier 'such as HDFS or S3, to store the completed log segments'; 'Apache Kafka doesn't provide an out-of-the-box RemoteStorageManager implementation.' Opened 3.9.0 announcement: 'Tiered storage is now production-ready in Kafka 3.9.'

final_text: Managed-Kafka SLAs vary: Amazon MSK gives service credits when a Multi-AZ cluster's monthly uptime falls below 99.9%, while Confluent Cloud offers up to 99.99% (Standard/Enterprise clusters with at least 2 eCKU, multi-zone Dedicated, Freight) and 99.5% for Basic.
note: Opened MSK SLA: Multi-AZ credit tiers start at 'Less than 99.9%'. Opened Confluent cluster types: 99.99% 'Requires 2 eCKU' for Standard/Enterprise; Dedicated 'require multi-zone deployments for the 99.99% SLA'; Basic 99.5%. Reworded for the eCKU condition.

final_text: MongoDB's data-modelling guide says duplicating data avoids joins on reads, but 'if the duplicated data is updated often, using a reference ... may be a better approach'.
note: Opened MongoDB embedding vs references: 'Duplicating data can remove the need to perform joins across multiple collections'; 'if the duplicated data is updated often, using a reference to link related data may be a better approach'. The ellipsis in the quote is accurate.

final_text: CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) means using a different model to update information than the model used to read it. Martin Fowler credits Greg Young, and notes it fits event-based systems and is often split into services that communicate with events.
note: Opened Fowler bliki CQRS: 'a pattern that I first heard described by Greg Young'; 'CQRS fits well with event-based programming models'; 'common to see CQRS system split into separate services communicating with Event Collaboration'. Fowler also warns 'for most systems CQRS adds risky complexity'.

final_text: Kinesis lets a reader start at TRIM_HORIZON (oldest retained record), LATEST, AT_TIMESTAMP, or at or after a specific sequence number.
note: Opened Kinesis GetShardIterator: TRIM_HORIZON 'the oldest data record in the shard', LATEST, AT_TIMESTAMP, AT_SEQUENCE_NUMBER, AFTER_SEQUENCE_NUMBER.

final_text: In the Python 3.15 docs, cProfile is a backward-compatible alias of profiling.tracing (a deterministic profiler). The docs recommend profiling.sampling for production debugging and profiling.tracing for development and testing.
note: Opened docs.python.org/3/library/profile.html, now the Python 3.15 docs: 'The cProfile module remains available as a backward-compatible alias to profiling.tracing'; 'profiling.sampling for production debugging with zero overhead'. Pinned the version, since this is new in 3.15.

final_text: Continuous (sampling) profilers are built to run everywhere: Datadog says its Continuous Profiler 'runs in production across all services' with minimal CPU and memory impact.
note: Opened Datadog profiler docs: 'Continuous Profiler runs in production across all services by using technologies such as JDK Flight Recorder', with minimal CPU and memory impact. Vendor page.

final_text: DRM restricts playback, but it cannot attribute a leak once the screen is recorded. Leakers are identified with forensic watermarking, which embeds an invisible viewer-specific mark in each copy.
note: Opened VdoCipher glossary (vendor page, secondary): 'Forensic watermarking embeds an invisible, viewer-specific or copy-specific identifier'; DRM 'cannot attribute a leak once a screen is recorded'. Accurate; a vendor-neutral source would be better.

final_text: In Knit Pro International v. State of NCT of Delhi (20 May 2022), India's Supreme Court held that Section 63 copyright infringement (6 months to 3 years plus fine) is cognizable and non-bailable.
note: Opened LiveLaw: 'offence under Section 63 of the Copyright Act is a cognizable and non-bailable offence', judgment 20 May 2022 (CrA 807 of 2022), 6 months to 3 years plus fine.

final_text: AWS says RDS Multi-AZ DB instance failovers 'are typically 60-120 seconds', and clients must reconnect because the DNS record changes.
note: Opened RDS Multi-AZ failover: 'Failover times are typically 60-120 seconds'; failover 'changes the Domain Name System (DNS) record ... you need to re-establish any existing connections'.

final_text: Cassandra describes its leaderless design as multi-master replication: every replica can accept writes, and conflicting updates are resolved by last-write-wins timestamps (so clocks need NTP).
note: Opened Cassandra Dynamo architecture: 'Multi-master replication using versioned data'; 'every replica can independently accept mutations'; 'last-write-wins model where every mutation is timestamped'; 'make sure a proper time synchronization process is running such as NTP'.

final_text: Go's GOMAXPROCS (default: number of CPU cores) limits how many goroutines execute at once; goroutines themselves start with a few-kilobyte stack, so hundreds of thousands can exist in one process.
note: Opened Go FAQ: GOMAXPROCS 'default value is the number of CPU cores available' and 'only affects how many goroutines can actually execute at once'; goroutine stack 'just a few kilobytes'; 'practical to create hundreds of thousands of goroutines'.

final_text: Jay Kreps, Kafka's co-creator, argues 'It's Okay To Store Data In Kafka' (2017): with retention set to forever or log compaction, data is kept for all time, so Kafka can be a system of record, though this means 'raising the bar for how you run it'.
note: Opened Confluent blog (Jay Kreps, 15 Sep 2017): title 'It's Okay To Store Data In Kafka'; 'raising the bar for how you run it, though'. The phrase 'does mean raising the bar' could not be confirmed verbatim, so the quote was trimmed.
